newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta debt/interbank market closing report.
newsitem.headline: Peseta debt/interbank market closing report.

text.p: The Spanish debt market ended substantially lower on Monday in line with other European bonds, with the new front-end June future contract losing more ground than March in its last trading day.
"The future fell sharply. There is more than one single factor pushing down the market," a dealer said. "There's a political factor in Italy, but that doesn't explain why Bunds are down".
He said the market was focusing on key U.S. data, such as U.S. CPI on Wednesday and then the March 25 FOMC, at which some are expecting a rate hike.
"Still I don't think even a 25 basis points hike should bother the market too much," another dealer added.
German finance minister Theo Waigel's remarks earlier this morning added further pressure to European markets, as they prompted dealers to worry about a possible delay in EMU.
Spain's yield curve steepened a bit, with the two- to 10-year spread widening to around 125 basis points from 120 bps, and dealers said it could offer value in the coming days.

"I expect it to steepen even more in the following days, as the short end should be less affected than the longer end by factors such as Euro pessimism and Fed blues," said Jose Antonio Mielgo at Bank of America in Madrid.
A very weak peseta prompted the Bank of Spain to intervene, and dealers reported it bought Spain's unit at around 84.85 per mark and later in the day at around 85.00 per mark.
The peseta ended at around 84.95/85.00 to the mark.
But while hefty currency reserves in Spain's central bank are considered enough to defend the peseta, and maintain short term money market rates, dealers were more pessimistic on the longer end.
"We saw some buying by a few insurance firms at the bottom end, but only for modest amounts," a dealer said.
The 10-year 7.35 percent benchmark ended at around 101 versus 102.24 at Friday's close.
"The 10-year yield could be pushed down to around 7.25 percent (versus current 7.17 percent) in a couple of weeks," said Bank of America's Mielgo.
